title: Separating a detector delay from an enzyme’s initial rate
stem:
A product detector has a known 10 s mixing delay. After that delay, enzyme X gives product concentrations 0, 12, 24, 35 and 43 µmol dm−3 at times 10, 20, 30, 40 and 60 s. A no-enzyme control remains at zero. The last substrate concentration is much lower than the initial concentration.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial rate using the first reliable 20 s interval and compare it with the mean rate from 10 to 60 s.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the decreasing slope without assuming that X is being consumed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Design a comparison of X at two temperatures that distinguishes a temperature effect from the detector delay.

steps.text: Use Δproduct/Δtime over 10–30 s: (24−0)/(30−10).
Initial rate = 1.20 µmol dm−3 s−1.
The 10–60 s mean is 43/50 = 0.860 µmol dm−3 s−1, lower than the initial rate.
Substrate depletion reduces the frequency of productive substrate–active-site encounters.
The enzyme is regenerated after catalysis; fewer substrate molecules can lower rate without lowering enzyme amount.
Equilibrate enzyme and substrate separately at each temperature, then mix using the same measured timing protocol.
Use equal enzyme/substrate concentrations, pH and volume and compare slopes over the same post-mixing initial interval.
Use independent replicate reaction mixtures and report their spread; include no-enzyme controls at both temperatures.

title: Recovery after pH treatment is different from recovery after heating
stem:
Identical enzyme samples are pretreated, then all are assayed at pH 7 and 25°C with excess substrate. Untreated control activities are 98, 100 and 102 units. Samples pretreated at pH 3 give 76, 80 and 84 units after neutralization. Samples heated at 80°C give 3, 4 and 5 units after cooling. One unit is the same product rate in every assay.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate mean recovered activity as a percentage of the control for each pretreatment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the assay conditions and recovery result matter when interpreting denaturation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that all molecules in the pH-treated sample are undamaged.

steps.text: Control mean = 100; pH-treated mean = 80; heated mean = 4.
Recovered activities are 80.0% and 4.00%, respectively.
Assaying all samples at the same pH and temperature removes immediate assay-condition differences.
Persistent loss after cooling is consistent with heat-induced disruption of the protein’s functional conformation and active site.
Substantial recovery after neutralization shows that low activity at pH 3 need not imply irreversible destruction; altered charges/interactions can be partly reversible.
The sample mean remains 20% below the control, so full recovery of the preparation is not demonstrated.
A mean activity cannot identify whether every molecule has lower activity or some molecules are inactive.
Use more independent samples and recovery-time measurements; the three replicates show variability but do not by themselves establish statistical significance.

title: A catalyst changes the barrier while the endpoint stays the same
stem:
The figure models the same catabolic reaction with and without an enzyme. Reactants have relative energy 20 kJ mol−1, products 5 kJ mol−1, and the two highest energies are 90 and 48 kJ mol−1. The horizontal coordinate is reaction progress, not time.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate both forward activation energies and the overall energy change.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain which curve is enzyme-catalysed and why more product per unit time is expected at the same temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the statements “the enzyme supplies the released energy” and “the graph shows a shorter reaction time”.

steps.text: Subtract reactant energy from each peak: 90−20 and 48−20.
The barriers are 70 and 28 kJ mol−1.
Overall products−reactants = 5−20 = −15 kJ mol−1.
The curve with peak 48 kJ mol−1 is enzyme-catalysed.
The lower activation barrier allows a larger fraction of substrate collisions to lead to reaction at the same temperature.
Both curves have the same reactant and product energies, so the enzyme does not supply the net released energy.
An enzyme is regenerated and provides an alternative catalytic pathway rather than being a consumed energy source.
The x-axis is reaction progress; a reaction duration cannot be read from it.

title: Correcting a seed respirometer for a drifting control
stem:
A sealed respirometer contains 2.00 g germinating seeds and a CO2 absorber separated from the seeds. A matched control contains glass beads of equal displaced volume and the same absorber. Over 12.0 min the capillary marker moves 18.0 mm towards the seed chamber and 3.0 mm towards the control chamber. The capillary internal cross-sectional area is 0.800 mm². Temperature is kept constant.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate corrected oxygen uptake in mm³ min−1 g−1, assuming marker movement measures gas-volume loss.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the functions of the absorber and control.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assess two improvements and one limitation when comparing seeds at 15°C and 25°C.

steps.text: Corrected displacement = 18.0−3.0 = 15.0 mm; volume = 15.0×0.800 = 12.0 mm³.
The absorber removes respiratory CO2 so oxygen consumption produces a measurable gas-volume decrease.
The bead control estimates shared non-biological pressure/volume drift without respiring tissue.
Allow each sealed apparatus to equilibrate at its test temperature before resetting the marker; temperature itself changes gas volume.
Use equal seed dry mass or a clearly defined mass basis, similar germination stage and independent replicate chambers.
Oxygen uptake estimates aerobic respiration under these conditions; it does not directly measure all ATP production or anaerobic respiration.

title: The same ATP demand can require different glucose consumption
stem:
A constructed yeast comparison uses equal cell numbers. In the oxygenated condition, 0.400 mmol glucose is consumed per hour. In the oxygen-free condition, 3.20 mmol is consumed per hour. For this model only, measured usable ATP yields are 28 ATP per glucose with oxygen and 2 ATP per glucose without oxygen; these are supplied experimental values, not universal yields.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate ATP production in mmol ATP h−1 for both conditions and the ratio of glucose consumption.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why a larger glucose consumption rate does not imply a larger ATP production rate.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the glucose-consumption rate needed to meet an ATP demand of 11.2 mmol h−1 without oxygen. Predict one consequence if that rate cannot be sustained, and distinguish cellular respiration from gas exchange.

steps.text: Multiply each glucose rate by its supplied ATP yield.
Oxygenated: 0.400×28 = 11.2 mmol ATP h−1; oxygen-free: 3.20×2 = 6.40 mmol ATP h−1.
Oxygen-free glucose consumption is 3.20/0.400 = 8.00 times as large.
Anaerobic respiration gives less ATP per glucose because breakdown is incomplete and energy remains in products.
The supplied yield difference exceeds the eightfold glucose-rate difference, so total ATP production is lower without oxygen.
Required glucose = 11.2/2 = 5.60 mmol h−1.
If glucose supply or the anaerobic pathway cannot support that rate, ATP-consuming processes such as active transport or biosynthesis must slow.
Cell respiration transfers chemical energy to ATP; ATP hydrolysis then supplies energy to cellular work rather than respiration being synonymous with gas exchange.

title: A light-response curve contains respiration as well as photosynthesis
stem:
A leaf chamber measures net CO2 uptake per leaf area. At light intensities 0, 100, 200, 400 and 800 µmol photons m−2 s−1, net uptake is −2, 1, 4, 7 and 7 µmol CO2 m−2 s−1. Assume leaf respiration releases 2 µmol CO2 m−2 s−1 throughout this short investigation. At intensity 800, raising external CO2 increases net uptake to 11.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate gross photosynthetic uptake at light intensities 0 and 400, and estimate the light compensation intensity by linear interpolation from 0 to 100.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what the plateau and additional CO2 treatment show about limiting factors.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate two assumptions needed before comparing gross photosynthesis across treatments.

steps.text: Gross photosynthesis = net uptake + respiratory release.
Gross rates are 0 and 9 µmol CO2 m−2 s−1.
Compensation occurs at (2/3)×100 = 66.7 µmol photons m−2 s−1.
Light is limiting on the rising part because increased intensity increases net uptake.
At high light, the rise from 7 to 11 after CO2 addition shows that CO2 availability limited uptake under the original conditions.
Respiration may change with leaf temperature or metabolic state, so the stated constant-respiration assumption should be checked.
Keep leaf area, temperature and water supply comparable; increased lamp heating can otherwise confound a light treatment.
Use independent leaves and replicated CO2 treatments; one response curve does not establish population-level significance.

title: One pigment band in one solvent is not a secure identification
stem:
The schematic chromatography strip shows distances from the origin. The solvent front moved 80 mm and bands A, B and C moved 20, 43 and 64 mm. Reference pigment P has Rf 0.54 in this solvent and Q has Rf 0.80. In a second solvent the sample band originally called B separates into two bands.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the three Rf values and identify the provisional matches.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the implication of B separating in the second solvent.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Design a stronger test linking a separated pigment to photosynthesis.

steps.text: Rf = distance moved by pigment / distance moved by solvent front.
B is provisionally consistent with P and C with Q in the first solvent.
The original B band can contain at least two components that travelled together in the first solvent.
An Rf match in one solvent is evidence for a possible identity, not proof of chemical purity or a unique pigment.
Run authentic standards and sample together under identical solvent, paper and temperature conditions.
Measure the isolated pigment’s absorption spectrum and compare wavelengths with a properly normalized photosynthetic action spectrum.
A correlation between absorption and action supports a role but does not prove the pigment alone drives every photosynthetic step; other pigments can transfer absorbed energy.

title: Comparing equal-photon action and absorption spectra
stem:
At 430, 480, 550, 620 and 680 nm, a pigment extract has relative absorbance 0.90, 0.55, 0.10, 0.40 and 0.80. Intact leaves supplied with equal photon flux at each wavelength produce oxygen at rates 18, 14, 4, 10 and 17 arbitrary units. Leaf area, temperature and CO2 are held constant.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare the two spectra using two paired observations.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the action-rate ratio at 430 versus 550 nm and explain why green light still gives a non-zero result.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that red photons are always the only useful greenhouse illumination.

steps.text: Both have relatively high values at 430 and 680 nm and a low value at 550 nm.
At 480 nm, absorbance is lower than at 680 nm (0.55 versus 0.80), and oxygen production is also lower (14 versus 17).
The oxygen-production ratio is 4.50.
The extract still absorbs some green light and intact leaves contain several pigments; low absorption does not mean no energy is absorbed.
Blue light also has a high measured action rate, so the data do not support an exclusively red requirement.
Equal photon flux makes this comparison meaningful, but these are selected wavelengths under one set of conditions; whole-growth responses need further testing.
Use replicated plants under equal total photon supply and controlled temperature/CO2, then measure growth or carbon gain rather than inferring it solely from one short-term rate.

title: Conduction speed and myelination need a controlled comparison
stem:
Four axon preparations have the following diameter, myelination and conduction speed: A, 2 µm, unmyelinated, 2 m s−1; B, 8 µm, unmyelinated, 8 m s−1; C, 2 µm, myelinated, 14 m s−1; D, 8 µm, myelinated, 56 m s−1. A stimulus is recorded 0.140 m along C after a short fixed equipment delay that has already been subtracted.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the conduction time along C and compare C with A.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use two comparisons to separate the effects of diameter and myelination.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a mixed-axon correlation cannot by itself measure the causal effect of diameter, and identify the basic path of a neural message.

steps.text: Time = distance/speed = 0.140/14.
At equal diameter, C conducts seven times as fast as A.
Among unmyelinated axons, increasing diameter from 2 to 8 µm increases speed from 2 to 8 m s−1.
At diameter 8 µm, myelination is associated with an increase from 8 to 56 m s−1.
Diameter and myelination both vary; a correlation using all four points confounds their separate contributions.
Use comparable axons with the same myelination status and control temperature when testing diameter effects.
Inputs are received through dendrites/cell body and an action potential propagates along the axon toward terminal synapses; detailed channel sequencing is not required here.

title: Calcium removal separates arrival from transmitter release
stem:
In a chemical synapse model, an action potential is detected at the presynaptic terminal in every treatment. Vesicle-fusion counts per terminal over the same interval are: normal external Ca2+, 24; Ca2+-free medium, 2; Ca2+-free medium plus acetylcholine applied directly to the postsynaptic membrane, 2. Postsynaptic depolarization occurs in the first and third treatments but not the second. The third treatment does not restore vesicle fusion.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage decrease in vesicle fusion on removing Ca2+.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce the stage impaired by calcium removal and explain the direct-acetylcholine result.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain normal transmission direction and evaluate what this experiment does not show.

steps.text: Vesicle fusion decreases by 91.7%.
Action-potential arrival is retained, but fusion falls; the evidence places the main impairment between arrival and transmitter release.
Ca2+ entry into the terminal normally triggers vesicle fusion and transmitter release.
Applied acetylcholine bypasses impaired presynaptic release and can still act on functional postsynaptic receptors.
Vesicles release transmitter from the presynaptic side; receptors on the postsynaptic membrane respond to diffusion across the cleft.
Binding of acetylcholine opens channels allowing positive ions to enter and depolarize the postsynaptic membrane.
Counts from one model do not establish universal effect size or prove every other presynaptic process is unaffected; independent terminals and controls are needed.

title: Blood chemistry coordinates ventilation and circulation
stem:
In a short model investigation, increased inspired CO2 raises arterial CO2 while oxygen is held near its starting value. At minutes 0, 2, 4 and 6, ventilation rates are 6, 9, 12 and 10 dm³ min−1 and heart rates are 70, 79, 88 and 82 min−1. At minute 4, arterial pH is lower than at minute 0. The gas treatment ends after minute 4.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage increase in ventilation and heart rate from minute 0 to minute 4.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain a feedback route linking elevated CO2 to increased ventilation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish this control from baroreceptor feedback and explain why both systems can affect the heart.

steps.text: Use (final−initial)/initial×100 for each variable.
Ventilation rises 100%; heart rate rises 25.7%.
More CO2 in blood increases acidity and lowers pH; chemoreceptors, including those in the brainstem, detect the change.
Respiratory centres in the brainstem send nerve signals to diaphragm and intercostal muscles, increasing ventilation.
Greater CO2 removal opposes the initial rise, so this component is negative feedback.
Baroreceptors in the carotid/aortic regions monitor blood pressure rather than directly monitoring CO2.
Chemoreceptor and baroreceptor input is integrated by the medulla, which adjusts cardiac activity through nerve signals.
Transport and ventilation must be coordinated to deliver oxygen and remove respiratory CO2; a matching time trend alone does not prove one measured rate directly causes the other.

title: A withdrawal reflex can survive loss of conscious sensation
stem:
The schematic shows a pain-withdrawal pathway with one spinal interneuron. Route S enters the spinal cord; route M leaves it. A separate ascending pathway carries information from the cord to the cerebral hemispheres. In a hypothetical lesion, the ascending pathway is interrupted above the entry level while S, the interneuron, M and the muscle remain functional.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Predict whether rapid withdrawal and conscious perception of this stimulus are retained, explaining the distinction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the effects of cutting S or cutting M in separate trials.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a nerve cross-section can contain both sensory and motor fibres and why the cerebellum has a different role.

steps.text: The local withdrawal reflex can remain, while conscious perception carried by the interrupted route is lost.
The spinal cord integrates the local sensory–interneuron–motor pathway without requiring a conscious decision first.
Conscious perception requires information to reach the appropriate cerebral regions.
Cutting S prevents this stimulus from reaching the spinal reflex circuit, so the specified withdrawal is absent.
Cutting M prevents the output reaching the flexor, so withdrawal is absent even if sensory information still reaches the cord.
A peripheral nerve is a bundle of axons; different fibres can carry sensory input toward the CNS and motor output away.
An impulse in an individual fibre has a defined propagating path; a mixed nerve is not one axon carrying both functions.
The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance, whereas the local spinal circuit can initiate this simple involuntary withdrawal.

title: Relative vaccine effectiveness differs from absolute risk reduction
stem:
In a constructed randomized trial, 10 000 participants receive a vaccine and 10 000 receive placebo. During the same follow-up, symptomatic infection occurs in 120 vaccinated and 300 placebo participants. Define relative effectiveness = 1−(vaccinated risk/placebo risk). A supplied 95% confidence interval for the risk ratio is 0.32–0.50; a ratio of 1 is the no-difference value. Allocation is concealed and outcome assessors are blinded.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate both infection risks, relative effectiveness and absolute risk reduction in percentage points.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Interpret the supplied confidence interval without using error-bar overlap as a test.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain two design strengths and one limit to generalization.

steps.text: Relative effectiveness = 1−0.012/0.030 = 0.600 = 60.0%.
Absolute reduction = 3.00%−1.20% = 1.80 percentage points.
The interval lies below the no-difference ratio of 1, supporting lower symptomatic risk for the vaccinated group under the stated analysis.
It does not mean that 95% of individuals have risk ratios in that interval or that protection is complete.
Random allocation reduces systematic baseline confounding, while concealed allocation limits selection into groups.
Blinded outcome assessment reduces differential classification of symptoms/infection.
The result applies to the studied population, outcome and follow-up; it alone does not establish the same effectiveness against every infection, future variant or time since vaccination.

title: A second exposure tests antigen-specific memory
stem:
A model organism receives antigen A at day 0. At day 28 it receives A again and a novel antigen B for the first time. Antibody concentrations to A peak at 20 units after the first dose and 120 units after the second. Antibody to B peaks at 24 units after its first dose. Antigen-specific assays do not cross-react.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio of the second A peak to its first peak and compare the response to A with B after day 28.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the cellular basis of this contrast.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate what antibody concentration alone cannot establish about protection.

steps.text: The second A peak is 6.00 times the first.
After day 28, A rises sooner and reaches a much higher peak than B, although both antigens are delivered at the same time.
The first A exposure selects A-specific lymphocytes, which proliferate and form plasma cells and memory cells.
A-specific memory cells remain and respond rapidly on re-exposure, producing many antibody-secreting cells.
B is novel, so its specific lymphocyte population must undergo a primary response; A memory is not automatically memory to unrelated B.
Binding antibodies do not necessarily all neutralize the pathogen; concentration alone is not a complete functional protection assay.
The model shows antigen-specific humoral memory but does not measure all cellular defences, exposure differences or duration of protection.

title: Replica patterns distinguish selection from a directed mutation claim
stem:
Colonies grow first on an antibiotic-free master plate. A sterile transfer copies their positions to two plates containing antibiotic. Resistant colonies repeatedly appear at matching positions, as shown. In a separate culture, resistant bacteria increase from 0.10% to 80.0% after many generations with antibiotic; total cell numbers and growth need not remain constant.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the replicated pattern supports resistance existing before antibiotic exposure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold increase in resistant proportion and its increase in percentage points.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain natural selection and antibiotic selectivity, and identify a limit of these data.

steps.text: Matching positions trace resistant descendants to the same original colonies on the antibiotic-free master plate.
Independent directed mutations caused by contact with the drug would not specifically predict repeated matching source positions.
Compare proportions using 80.0/0.10, while percentage points use subtraction.
The resistant proportion increases 800-fold; the increase is 79.9 percentage points.

title: Immigration can bias a capture–mark–recapture estimate
stem:
In a closed-population model, 80 animals are captured, marked and released. After mixing, 100 animals are captured and 20 are marked. Use N≈MC/R, where M is originally marked, C is the second sample and R is its marked count. A second scenario adds unmarked immigrants before recapture, while marked residents remain; the estimate then concerns an intended original resident population.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

steps.text: Estimated population = 400 animals; the sample is 80.0% unmarked.
Adding unmarked animals reduces the marked proportion R/C, if the capture process is otherwise comparable.
Because N≈M/(R/C), the estimate increases and overestimates the original resident population.
Marks should remain detectable and not change survival, behaviour or capture probability.
Marked animals should mix with unmarked animals, and individuals should have similar capture probabilities for the estimator used.
Births, deaths and boundary movements should be negligible between occasions for a closed-population interpretation.
A short pilot can compare marked versus unmarked survival/capture or assess mixing by recapture locations; repeat sampling with a justified design rather than assuming closure.

title: Unequal habitat areas require a weighted quadrat estimate
stem:
A 1200 m² reserve contains 900 m² dry habitat and 300 m² damp habitat. Five randomly located 1.00 m² quadrats in the dry area contain 1, 2, 2, 3 and 2 plants; five in the damp area contain 8, 10, 12, 9 and 11. Quadrats do not overlap. The schematic shows the habitat boundary; points are sampling positions, not individual plants.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate total plants using the two habitat means and compare it with pooling all ten quadrats without weighting.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the source of the discrepancy.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Propose a stronger estimate with uncertainty and define the sampling unit.

steps.text: Dry mean = 2.00 m−2; damp mean = 10.0 m−2; multiply each by its habitat area.
Stratified estimate = 2×900 + 10×300 = 4800 plants.
Unweighted pooled mean = 6.00 m−2 gives 7200 plants, an overestimate of 2400.
Half the sampled quadrats come from damp habitat although damp habitat is only one quarter of the reserve.
Pooling without area weighting over-represents the high-density damp habitat.
Use more independently randomized quadrat positions in each habitat, retaining area weights; effort can be allocated by area and observed variation.
The quadrat is the sampling unit; treating each counted plant as an independent spatial sample would inflate replication.
Report habitat variation and uncertainty of the weighted estimate; random positioning reduces selection bias but does not ensure one small sample is exact.

title: Species association is evidence to investigate, not proof of mutualism
stem:
In 100 independently sampled quadrats, species X and Y are both present in 30, X alone in 10, Y alone in 20 and neither in 40. Test independence with χ²=Σ(O−E)²/E; expected count E=(row total×column total)/100. Use 1 degree of freedom and critical χ²=3.84 at p=0.05. The figure plots the four observed counts. Both species might also respond to soil moisture.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the four expected counts and χ², then state the statistical conclusion under the supplied test.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the association and explain why it does not prove mutualism.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Design a test that distinguishes a direct beneficial interaction from the shared-moisture explanation.

steps.text: X present total=40; Y present total=50, so expected counts are 20, 20, 30 and 30 in the stated order.
16.7 exceeds 3.84, so reject independence at the stated threshold.
Co-occurrence is more frequent than expected under independence: 30 observed versus 20 expected.
Shared preference for moisture could generate the pattern without either species benefiting the other.
Randomize addition/removal or presence/absence of X in matched plots while independently controlling or crossing soil moisture treatments.
Measure Y survival/growth/reproduction, use replicate independent plots and include handling controls.
To claim mutualism, also test a benefit of Y to X; association or a one-way benefit is insufficient.

title: Energy must be converted to production before transfer efficiency
stem:
All fluxes in this constructed grassland budget are kJ m−2 year−1. Grass net primary production is 12 000. Herbivores ingest 2400, egest 900 and use 1100 in respiration; the remaining assimilated energy becomes production. Predators ingest 180 of herbivore production. No other herbivore losses are included.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

steps.text: Assimilation = 2400−900 = 1500; production = 1500−1100.
Herbivore production = 400 kJ m−2 year−1.
Production transfer efficiency = 400/12 000×100 = 3.33%.
Predators ingest 45.0% of herbivore production.
Predator egestion and respiration have not been subtracted, so predator production cannot be calculated from ingestion alone.
Unconsumed plant biomass and herbivore egesta can enter detrital food webs and provide substrates for decomposers.
Respiratory energy is dissipated as heat and is not recycled back into chemical energy by decomposers; elements can be recycled.

title: A carbon budget separates plant production from ecosystem storage
stem:
A field has annual gross carbon fixation 900 g C m−2 year−1. Producer respiration releases 360 and respiration by consumers/decomposers releases 450 in the same units. Harvest exports 40. Other imports/exports and changes in dissolved pools are negligible. Define net ecosystem production before harvest = gross fixation minus all ecosystem respiration.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a

NPP = 540 and net ecosystem production = 90 g C m−2 year−1.
After harvest the stock increases by 90−40 = 50 g C m−2 year−1.

title: A statin-like inhibitor changes substrate competition
stem:
A purified enzyme has model rate v=120S/(4+S) without inhibitor and v=120S/(12+S) with inhibitor I. S is in mmol dm−3 and v in µmol min−1. Define Vmax as the limiting rate at very large S, and K½ as the substrate concentration giving half that limiting rate. The inhibitor is a reversible active-site-binding compound used as a statin-like model; the equation and definitions are supplied, not recall requirements.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine Vmax and K½ in both treatments, then calculate the rates at S=4.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why high substrate concentration reduces this inhibitor’s effect.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Contrast the mechanism and high-substrate prediction with reversible allosteric non-competitive inhibition.

steps.text: Both expressions approach 120 as S becomes very large; half-rate requires S equal to the constant added to S in the denominator.
Vmax = 120 µmol min−1 in both; K½ = 4 and 12 mmol dm−3.
At S=4, rates are 60.0 without I and 30.0 µmol min−1 with I.
Substrate and inhibitor bind reversibly to the active site, so they compete for the same enzyme population.
Increasing substrate increases the chance that an active site is occupied by substrate rather than inhibitor; the same limiting rate can be approached.
An allosteric inhibitor binds a distinct specific site and changes enzyme conformation, impairing catalysis.
Substrate cannot simply displace it from that distinct site, so high substrate does not fully restore the uninhibited maximum in the non-competitive model.
The supplied fitted equations establish the model’s rate predictions; real samples need replicate initial-rate data and appropriate binding evidence before a mechanistic classification is claimed.

title: End-product feedback regulates a pathway before substrate is wasted
stem:
A simplified pathway converts threonine through intermediates to isoleucine. In separate assays of its first enzyme E1, activity is 10.0 units without added isoleucine, 3.0 with isoleucine, 3.2 with isoleucine plus tenfold threonine, and 9.6 after isoleucine is removed. E2 remains at 10.0 units. A binding experiment places isoleucine at a site distinct from E1’s active site.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate inhibition of E1 in the isoleucine treatment and percentage activity recovered after removal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why these results support reversible feedback inhibition of E1.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the advantage of targeting an early enzyme and compare this pathway with a metabolic cycle.

steps.text: Inhibition = (10.0−3.0)/10.0×100; recovered activity = 9.6/10.0×100.
E1 is inhibited by 70.0%; activity after removal is 96.0% of control.
Isoleucine is a pathway end product that specifically suppresses an earlier enzyme, reducing further synthesis when product accumulates.
Binding at a distinct site and little rescue by extra threonine support allosteric rather than direct active-site competition.
Recovery after removal supports reversible inhibition rather than permanent destruction of most enzyme.
Suppressing an early committed step avoids spending substrate and energy making unneeded downstream intermediates.
The depicted pathway is linear because its end product does not regenerate its starting substrate as part of the sequence.
In a cycle such as the Krebs or Calvin cycle, a starting acceptor is regenerated, allowing repeated operation while inputs enter and products leave.

title: Washout distinguishes a covalent inhibitor from reversible binding
stem:
Purified bacterial cell-wall cross-linking enzyme is incubated with a penicillin-like compound for 0, 5 or 10 min, then the free compound is removed before assay with abundant substrate. Activities are 90, 40 and 12 units. A matched no-compound sample remains at 90 units after the same handling. Analysis detects a covalent compound–enzyme adduct at the active site after washout. All conclusions concern this specified enzyme model.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate percentage loss of activity after 10 min and explain why a no-compound handling control is needed.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a mechanism-based inhibitor can produce the persistent loss.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict two outcomes and evaluate a limit of the assay.

steps.text: Activity loss = 86.7%.
The matched control tests whether incubation and compound-removal procedures themselves damage or remove enzyme.
The enzyme interacts with the inhibitor at its active site and catalysis leads to a chemical change/covalent adduct that inactivates the site.
Removing free compound does not remove the covalently bound adduct, so existing modified enzyme remains inactive.
This differs from a reversible competitive inhibitor, which can dissociate and be removed or outcompeted.
Adding more substrate after washout will not simply restore activity of the covalently inactivated sites.
Supplying newly synthesized unmodified enzyme can restore catalytic capacity if the free inhibitor has been removed.
A purified-enzyme result does not alone establish a dose that is effective or safe in an organism; entry, metabolism and other targets are not measured.

title: Metabolic heat is a rate normalized to the amount of living material
stem:
Two yeast preparations are tested in insulated calorimeters of effective heat capacity 420 J °C−1. Preparation A contains 0.500 g dry biomass and warms by 0.80°C in 10.0 min; B contains 1.00 g and warms by 1.20°C. A matched killed-yeast blank warms by 0.10°C in each run. Use heat Q=CΔT and subtract the blank before normalizing. Heat loss is initially assumed negligible.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the corrected heat-production rates per gram for A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why B warming more does not show greater activity per unit biomass and why heat accompanies metabolism.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish intracellular from extracellular catalysis and evaluate the heat-loss assumption.

steps.text: Corrected temperature rises are 0.70 and 1.10°C; heats are 294 and 462 J.
B contains twice as much biomass; its greater total heat can coexist with a lower mass-specific rate.
Metabolic energy transfer is not 100% efficient in capture as useful chemical work, and energy is dissipated as heat.
Glycolysis and Krebs-cycle reactions occur inside cells, whereas secreted digestive enzymes can catalyse reactions outside cells.
Heat leaving the calorimeter makes measured warming underestimate the true heat produced, even after subtracting a blank.

Calibrate the apparatus, use comparable starting temperatures and mixing, and obtain independent biological replicates; an identical blank drift does not guarantee identical heat loss in different-temperature runs.

title: Glycolysis has an investment phase before its net ATP return
stem:
A glycolysis model starts with 1.00 mmol glucose in the cytoplasm. Two ATP are used per glucose before cleavage into two 3-carbon molecules. Subsequent reactions form two ATP and one reduced NAD per 3-carbon molecule and end with pyruvate. The diagram tracks carbon units, not named intermediate molecules.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the linked oxidation and reduction in the pathway.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the direct effect of a treatment that prevents ADP from accepting phosphate, assuming all other components are initially present.

steps.text: Each glucose yields two 3-carbon branches; apply the supplied yield to both branches.
Pyruvate = 2.00 mmol; gross ATP formed = 4.00 mmol; net ATP gain = 4.00−2.00 = 2.00 mmol.
Reduced NAD formed = 2.00 mmol.
An organic intermediate is oxidized by transfer of hydrogen/electrons to NAD.
NAD is reduced and can carry reducing power to later reactions; it is not the final carbon product.
The ATP-producing substrate-level phosphorylation reactions cannot continue normally without usable ADP.
Gross ATP production and net gain fall; ATP used early must not be counted again as a net product.
The model identifies cytoplasmic carbon breakdown but does not imply that glycolysis alone fully oxidizes glucose or requires oxygen directly.

title: Fermentation restores an electron acceptor rather than adding ATP
stem:
A sealed cytoplasmic system starts with glucose, glycolytic enzymes, ADP/phosphate and a total NAD pool of 0.200 mmol, all initially oxidized. Each glucose converted to two pyruvates reduces two NAD. If reduced NAD is not reoxidized, glycolysis stops when all NAD is reduced. The system first lacks a fermentation enzyme; a lactate-producing enzyme is then added. This enzyme transfers reducing power from reduced NAD to pyruvate and forms no ATP directly.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the maximum glucose amount processed before NAD exhaustion in the initial system.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why lactate production permits continued glycolytic ATP generation without oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare this with anaerobic respiration in yeast and predict carbon-containing products from 0.500 mmol glucose in each pathway.

steps.text: Two NAD are reduced per glucose, so glucose limit = 0.200/2.
Maximum glucose processed = 0.100 mmol, if all initial NAD is oxidized.
Reduction of pyruvate to lactate reoxidizes reduced NAD to NAD.
The regenerated NAD can accept hydrogen/electrons in glycolysis again, so glycolysis can continue making its net ATP.
The lactate step itself gives no extra ATP; its role is coenzyme recycling rather than complete oxidation of pyruvate.
The lactate pathway yields 1.00 mmol lactate without releasing carbon as CO2 in this conversion.
The yeast pathway yields 1.00 mmol ethanol and 1.00 mmol CO2; pyruvate is decarboxylated before the remaining 2-carbon compound is reduced.
Both pathways regenerate NAD, while the different final carbon products retain energy that has not been completely released.

title: Acetyl input is balanced by carbon loss while an acceptor returns
stem:
In an aerobic mitochondrial model, each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO2 during the link reaction, producing a 2-carbon acetyl group and one reduced NAD. One Krebs-cycle turn joins this acetyl group to 4-carbon oxaloacetate, forms 6-carbon citrate, releases two CO2 and regenerates oxaloacetate. Per turn the supplied accounting is three reduced NAD, one other reduced carrier and one ATP equivalent. Do not infer which specific acetyl carbons leave in the first turn.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For 1.50 mmol pyruvate entering the link reaction, calculate CO2 released by link plus complete cycle turns and the total reduced NAD formed in these two stages.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why oxaloacetate is required but is not consumed once per cycle turn.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate two conclusions about the carbon and energy accounting.

steps.text: There are 1.50 mmol link reactions and 1.50 mmol cycle turns.
Reduced NAD = 1.50×(1+3) = 6.00 mmol.
Oxaloacetate accepts the 2-carbon acetyl group to form citrate at the start.
Later cycle reactions regenerate the 4-carbon acceptor, permitting another acetyl group to enter.
Carbon numbers balance through 4+2=6 followed by loss of two CO2 and regeneration of a 4-carbon molecule.
The two CO2 in a turn are not sufficient evidence that the newly entered acetyl carbon atoms were both released in that same turn; positional tracing would be needed.
Much energy is transferred to reduced carriers rather than all being captured directly as the one ATP equivalent; these electrons can feed later aerobic processes.

title: Blocking ATP synthase differs from making the membrane leaky
stem:
The inner mitochondrial membrane schematic has intermembrane space above and matrix below. X moves protons upward using energy from electron transfer; Y allows protons downward and has its catalytic head below. In a supplied experiment, control oxygen uptake, ATP production and proton-gradient size are 10, 30 and 8 relative units. Blocking Y gives 2, 0 and 12; adding a proton leak to the blocked preparation gives 13, 0 and 1. Other substrates remain available.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify X and Y by function and explain where ATP is produced.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why blocking Y increases the gradient but lowers oxygen uptake, and why the leak changes oxygen uptake without restoring ATP.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the control ATP/oxygen-unit ratio and evaluate its use outside this model.

steps.text: X represents electron-transfer-linked proton pumping; Y is ATP synthase.
Protons are pumped from matrix to intermembrane space, then flow back down their electrochemical gradient through ATP synthase.
The catalytic head faces the matrix, where ADP is phosphorylated to ATP.
Blocking proton return prevents ATP synthesis and allows a steep gradient to accumulate, opposing further proton pumping/electron flow.
A leak dissipates the gradient so electron flow and oxygen consumption can accelerate again.
Proton return through a nonspecific leak bypasses the blocked synthase, so ATP synthesis is not restored.
The control ratio is 3.00 supplied ATP units per supplied oxygen unit.
These are relative experimental units under particular conditions, not a universal ATP yield per oxygen molecule or per glucose.

title: Oxygen demand follows pairs of electrons accepted at the chain’s end
stem:
In a mitochondrial preparation, 0.600 mmol reduced NAD is oxidized completely through an electron transport chain. Each reduced NAD supplies one pair of electrons. The terminal reaction is O2+4e−+4H+→2H2O. Ignore other electron donors. A separate preparation lacks oxygen but starts with the same amount of oxidized NAD and substrate.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate electron amount, minimum oxygen consumption and water formation for complete oxidation of the reduced NAD.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why oxygen removal can slow the Krebs cycle even though oxygen is not a reactant in each cycle step.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that adding more ADP alone solves the oxygen-free limitation.

steps.text: 0.600 mmol reduced NAD supplies 1.20 mmol electrons.
O2 required = 1.20/4 = 0.300 mmol.
Water formed = 2×0.300 = 0.600 mmol.
Without the terminal electron acceptor, electron carriers cannot continue transferring electrons at the same rate.
Reduced NAD is not reoxidized sufficiently, so oxidized NAD becomes limiting for dehydrogenation reactions in the link reaction and Krebs cycle.
This is indirect coupling through the redox carrier pool rather than oxygen being incorporated at every cycle step.
More ADP supplies a phosphorylation substrate but does not provide the missing terminal electron acceptor.
An alternative NAD-regenerating fermentation route could support glycolysis in suitable cells, but would not restore this oxygen-dependent mitochondrial electron flow.

title: A respiratory quotient can estimate a supplied substrate mixture
stem:
For this constructed substrate-mixture model, complete oxidation of carbohydrate consumes 1 mol O2 per mol CO2 produced, whereas the chosen lipid substrate produces 0.700 mol CO2 per mol O2. Let f be the fraction of total oxygen uptake attributable to carbohydrate; then mixture RQ=CO2/O2=f(1.00)+(1−f)(0.700). Measured rates are 0.850 mmol CO2 min−1 and 1.00 mmol O2 min−1. These relationships and the linear oxygen-weighting assumption are supplied.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate RQ and f, clearly stating what the resulting fraction measures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the fraction is not necessarily 50% of substrate mass or ATP production.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the aerobic roles of carbon compounds and oxygen, and evaluate one assumption of the mixture estimate.

steps.text: f=0.500; 50.0% of oxygen uptake is assigned to carbohydrate oxidation in this model.
The model weights by oxygen uptake; different substrates consume different amounts of oxygen per gram or molecule.
ATP yield depends on the pathway and coupling efficiency, which are not specified as equal for the two substrates.
Carbon substrates are oxidized and transfer reducing power to carriers; oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the respiratory electron-transfer process.
Lipids as well as carbohydrates can provide substrates for aerobic respiration after conversion into pathway inputs.

Incomplete oxidation, changing body CO2 stores or another substrate could break the supplied two-component relationship; gas exchange alone does not uniquely identify every substrate without the stated assumptions.

title: An artificial thylakoid gradient can drive ATP synthesis in darkness
stem:
The schematic represents a sealed thylakoid membrane. Stroma is above and lumen below. X uses light-driven electron transfer to move H+ into the lumen; Y lets H+ return to the stroma and has its catalytic head facing the stroma. In an artificial experiment, lumen pH is 5.00 and external stroma-side pH is 8.00 before light is removed. ADP and phosphate are available on the stroma side. For the supplied device only, 3 H+ through Y are required per ATP and 120 nmol H+ can flow before the gradient dissipates. Ignore electrical potential when calculating the concentration ratio.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial lumen/stroma proton concentration ratio and the maximum ATP from the supplied proton amount.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why ATP can briefly form in darkness and identify X and Y.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the effect of a membrane proton leak and explain the importance of Y’s orientation.

steps.text: The ratio is 10^(−5)/10^(−8)=10³; ATP amount is 120/3.
Lumen [H+] is 1000 times stroma [H+]; maximum ATP = 40.0 nmol.
X is light-driven proton pumping linked to electron transport; Y is ATP synthase.
The stored electrochemical proton gradient provides the driving force for H+ movement through ATP synthase; light is not directly used by the catalytic head.
ATP formation can continue briefly until the gradient dissipates, but cannot be sustained without restoring a gradient.
A leak lets H+ return without passing through ATP synthase, reducing the ATP yield from the stored gradient.
The catalytic head must face the stroma-side ADP/phosphate pool in this preparation; reversing orientation changes access and the direction of coupled synthesis.
The stated 3 H+/ATP belongs to this constructed device and is not asserted as a universal intact-chloroplast stoichiometry.

title: Cyclic electron flow can meet an ATP shortfall without making NADPH
stem:
For a constructed chloroplast model, fixing 3 CO2 into one net triose phosphate requires 9 ATP and 6 reduced NADP. A non-cyclic electron-flow run makes 6 reduced NADP and 6 ATP. An added cyclic run returns electrons to the transfer chain and makes ATP but no net reduced NADP or oxygen. These numerical yields are supplied for this preparation; they are not universal photon or proton yields.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the ATP shortfall and the ATP:reduced-NADP ratio needed by carbon fixation versus that supplied by the non-cyclic run.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how cyclic electron flow can address this mismatch.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the source of electrons and oxygen production in non-cyclic flow with cyclic flow.

steps.text: ATP shortfall = 9−6; required ratio = 9/6; supplied ratio = 6/6.
Shortfall = 3 ATP units; required ratio 1.50, supplied ratio 1.00.
Excited electrons from photosystem I return to the electron-transfer pathway rather than reducing NADP.
Electron flow supports proton-gradient formation and ATP synthesis without net NADP reduction.
It can add the missing ATP without adding more reducing power than the stated carbon-fixation demand.
Non-cyclic flow obtains replacement electrons by splitting water at photosystem II; oxygen is a product of that water oxidation.
Non-cyclic electrons eventually reduce NADP after excitation at photosystem I, rather than returning to the same route.
Cyclic flow alone does not split water or generate net oxygen; its ATP output cannot be inferred from oxygen evolution alone.

title: The Calvin cycle exports one carbon product while regenerating its acceptor
stem:
A Calvin-cycle model fixes 3 CO2 using 3 RuBP molecules, each containing 5 carbons. The resulting unstable products give 6 GP molecules, each with 3 carbons. Reduction forms 6 TP molecules, each with 3 carbons. One TP is exported and the other five regenerate the 3 RuBP. For this model, reduction uses 6 ATP and 6 reduced NADP; regeneration uses 3 further ATP.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Check carbon conservation through fixation, reduction/export and regeneration.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate ATP and reduced NADP required for a net pair of exported TP, and explain why the model has net gain despite being cyclic.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the roles of rubisco and the light-dependent reactions.

steps.text: Initial carbon = 3×5+3×1=18; six GP and six TP each contain 6×3=18 carbons.
Five retained TP contain 15 carbons, exactly enough for three 5-carbon RuBP.
One exported TP contains the three newly fixed carbons in the net balance.
Two net TP require two sets of the supplied 3-CO2 operation.
ATP = 2×(6+3)=18; reduced NADP = 2×6=12.
The acceptor is regenerated, while extra carbon enters as CO2 and some carbon leaves as product; cyclic acceptor regeneration does not mean zero net input/output.
Rubisco catalyses fixation of CO2 by reaction with RuBP; the products form GP.
Light-dependent processes supply ATP and reduced NADP for GP reduction and RuBP regeneration; they do not supply CO2 carbon.
GP and TP are different oxidation states, so ATP alone without reducing power cannot complete the stated conversion.

title: A dark transition reveals which Calvin intermediate accumulates
stem:
An illuminated chloroplast model reaches a steady state, then light is switched off at t=0 while CO2 remains available. At t=0, 5, 15 and 30 s, GP amounts are 20, 35, 50 and 50 nmol, while TP amounts are 20, 14, 7 and 4 nmol. ATP and reduced NADP rapidly decline. The early interval allows some residual RuBP fixation, but does not assume infinite RuBP stores.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the GP:TP ratio before the change and at 30 s and describe the paired changes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the early accumulation of GP and falling TP.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the GP plateau and evaluate a proposed rescue using CO2 alone.

steps.text: The ratio rises from 1.00 to 12.5.
GP increases then plateaus, whereas TP falls throughout the sampled period.
Loss of light stops sustained ATP/reduced-NADP supply, limiting conversion of GP to TP.
Residual RuBP can still be fixed briefly, adding GP while its reduction is slowed.
Existing TP continues to be used/exported or redirected into regeneration, so its pool can decline.
Without sufficient ATP-supported regeneration, RuBP becomes limiting, so continued GP production cannot be sustained indefinitely.
Extra CO2 alone does not replace ATP or reducing power, so it cannot restore the complete light-coupled cycle.
Pool sizes show the balance of formation and consumption, not a direct measurement of every reaction flux; use additional time-resolved ATP/RuBP measurements to test the explanation.

title: A selective electron donor tests a photosystem block
stem:
A constructed preparation has two light-absorbing photosystems in sequence. A treatment prevents water-derived electrons entering photosystem II but leaves photosystem I and its downstream NADP reduction machinery intact. Under illumination, oxygen evolution falls from 8 to 0 units and reduced-NADP production from 16 to 0. A supplied artificial donor that gives electrons directly to photosystem I restores reduced-NADP production to 10 units, while oxygen remains zero. The donor’s chemistry need not be recalled.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the fraction of control reduced-NADP production restored by the donor and explain why oxygen is not restored.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what the rescue establishes about the remaining light-dependent pathway.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate two claims about ATP and carbon fixation from these results.

steps.text: Reduced-NADP production is restored to 62.5% of control.
The artificial donor bypasses the blocked water/PSII entry; it does not split water, so it does not restore the source of oxygen.
Photosystem I can still use light excitation to support downstream reduction of NADP when it receives replacement electrons.
The original loss of reduced NADP is therefore consistent with lack of electron supply, not necessarily destruction of every downstream component.
Restored reduced NADP alone does not quantify ATP formation; electron routing and proton movement also need measurement.
Calvin-cycle carbon fixation needs ATP as well as reduced NADP, so 62.5% reducing-power rescue does not prove 62.5% carbon-fixation rescue.
Confirm selectivity with independent controls for light absorption, donor effects and component integrity; rescue is strong pathway evidence but is conditional on the stated bypass.

title: Conditioned medium separates bacterial density from its signal
stem:
Vibrio fischeri is used in a constructed quorum-sensing investigation. Low-density cells emit 2 light units per 10⁶ cells. Adding sterile-filtered medium from a high-density culture gives 40 units, while fresh medium gives 3. A signal-degrading treatment applied to conditioned medium reduces the effect to 4 units; heat-inactivated degrading treatment gives 38. Cell numbers, nutrients and oxygen are matched during the short assay.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold response to untreated conditioned medium relative to low-density cells and compare the two degrading treatments.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the results support quorum sensing through a diffusible ligand.

title: Receptor location must match how a ligand crosses a membrane
stem:
In a constructed animal-cell model, hydrophilic protein ligand P remains outside intact cells and binds receptor R in the plasma membrane. Steroid S enters the cell and binds an intracellular receptor. Introducing the S receptor into a previously unresponsive cell gives an S-dependent increase in a target transcript, provided its DNA response sequence is intact. Cells with a mutated response sequence bind S but do not increase this transcript.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce why S binding is not sufficient for this transcript response.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the receptor-introduction experiment as evidence of target-cell specificity.

steps.text: Hydrophilic P does not readily cross the hydrophobic bilayer, so its binding site must be exposed extracellularly on R.
The membrane-spanning portion of R has hydrophobic surfaces compatible with the bilayer, while aqueous exposed regions are relatively hydrophilic.
Steroid S can cross the bilayer and bind a receptor in cytoplasm or nucleus.
The activated intracellular receptor must interact with a specific DNA sequence to regulate transcription.
The mutated sequence allows ligand binding but removes the downstream DNA-dependent response in this model.
Gaining a response after receptor introduction supports receptor availability as one determinant of whether a cell is a target.
The DNA-sequence result shows that a receptor is not sufficient without compatible downstream machinery.
Include empty-vector controls and matched receptor expression/cell viability; introduced receptors can differ from normal physiological amounts.

title: Bypass rescue orders an adrenaline signalling pathway
stem:
A constructed liver-cell pathway links adrenaline receptor binding to a G protein, production of cAMP and a measured response. Response units are: adrenaline alone, 100; adrenaline plus receptor blocker, 8; receptor blocker plus membrane-permeable cAMP analogue, 92; adrenaline plus inhibitor of an enzyme downstream of cAMP, 6; downstream inhibitor plus cAMP analogue, 7. Assume the blockers have their stated selective targets. The cAMP analogue acts like intracellular cAMP.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

steps.text: The receptor acts upstream of cAMP because adding a cAMP analogue largely bypasses receptor blockade.
The second blocked enzyme acts downstream of cAMP because adding the analogue does not rescue its inhibition.
Supported order: adrenaline receptor → G protein/cAMP generation → downstream enzyme → response.
Recovery relative to control = 92/100×100.
Recovery = 92.0% of the control response.
Adrenaline is the extracellular first messenger; intracellular cAMP relays the receptor-triggered signal to downstream targets.
Removing adrenaline and degrading cAMP or reversing downstream activation can terminate signalling.
The ordering depends on selective inhibition and analogue access; off-target toxicity or unequal delivery could create misleading failure of rescue.

title: Insulin binding and intracellular phosphorylation are separate steps
stem:
In a constructed muscle-cell model, insulin binds normally to wild-type and mutant receptors. After insulin treatment, wild-type cells show receptor-associated tyrosine phosphorylation and 80 surface glucose transporters per measured membrane patch. Mutant cells lack this phosphorylation and show 20, the untreated baseline. An experimental downstream activation bypass restores 72 surface transporters in mutant cells. Total cellular transporter number is unchanged during the short assay.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how insulin reception normally increases glucose transport capacity.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the fold surface increase in wild type and the fraction of the insulin-induced increase rescued by the bypass.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Deduce a location for the mutant defect and evaluate the result.

steps.text: Insulin binds the extracellular portion of a receptor in the plasma membrane.
Binding activates intracellular tyrosine phosphorylation and a downstream signalling sequence.
Transporter-containing vesicles move to and fuse with the plasma membrane, increasing available surface glucose transporters.
Wild-type fold = 80/20; rescued increase fraction = (72−20)/(80−20).
Wild-type surface count rises 4.00-fold; 86.7% of the induced increase is rescued.
Normal binding but absent phosphorylation places the defect after ligand binding and at/before receptor-associated kinase signalling.
Downstream bypass rescue shows that the vesicle/transporter machinery retains substantial function.
Surface redistribution, not rapid synthesis of new transporter protein, explains unchanged total count; the model does not prove every possible downstream target is normal.

title: Oestradiol feedback depends on concentration and target-cell context
stem:
A supplied model concerns oestradiol-responsive GnRH-secreting hypothalamic cells. GnRH promotes a hormonal cascade that increases ovarian oestradiol. Relative GnRH output after equal exposure is 100 without oestradiol, 60 at a moderate sustained concentration and 150 at a high sustained concentration. Receptor-blocked cells remain near 100 in both hormone treatments. The model explicitly supplies a switch from negative to positive feedback at high sustained oestradiol; it does not assume that every tissue has this response.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: b

steps.text: Use (treated−100)/100×100.
Moderate concentration: −40.0%; high sustained concentration: +50.0%.
Oestradiol enters the cell and activates an intracellular receptor that can bind specific DNA sequences and alter transcription.
In the supplied moderate-concentration model, reduced upstream GnRH output opposes further stimulation: negative feedback.
In the supplied high sustained condition, increased GnRH output amplifies upstream stimulation: positive feedback.
The demonstrated target is the hypothalamic GnRH cell, and response also depends on receptor expression and downstream gene-regulatory context.
Oestradiol is a steroid capable of membrane entry; intracellular receptor action is consistent with the stated gene-regulatory mechanism.
Receptor blockade supports dependence on the receptor, but independent controls for blocker specificity and cell viability are needed before excluding other causes.

title: Progesterone changes transcription before a secretory response
stem:
A constructed endometrial-cell model measures production of a new target transcript and its encoded secreted protein after progesterone is added. At 0, 1, 3 and 6 h, transcript-production rates are 3, 9, 12 and 12 units, while accumulated secreted protein is 0, 1, 7 and 20 units. A selective block of receptor–DNA binding prevents the transcript increase but does not alter progesterone entry. Cell number and viability are matched.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum transcript-rate fold increase and compare the timing of transcript and secreted-protein responses.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain a mechanism connecting progesterone to the target transcript.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the two response variables measure the same quantity and identify a stronger causal test of the protein link.

steps.text: Maximum transcript-production rate is 4.00 times baseline.
Transcript rate rises by 1 h and reaches a plateau by 3 h, while secreted protein continues to accumulate to 6 h.
Progesterone enters the endometrial cell and binds its intracellular receptor.
The activated receptor binds a specific DNA sequence and regulates transcription of a target gene.
Blocking receptor–DNA binding can therefore prevent increased transcription even when hormone entry remains normal.
Transcript-production rate is a rate, whereas secreted protein is an accumulated amount; their numerical values cannot be compared as if they were the same units.
Protein accumulation also depends on translation, secretion and degradation, so a transcription plateau does not require a protein-amount plateau.

title: Persistent ligand binding can coexist with feedback adaptation
stem:
In a constructed receptor/cAMP pathway, a constant adrenaline treatment keeps receptor occupancy near 80%. cAMP is 1 unit before treatment, 10 at 1 min, 4 at 4 min and 2 at 8 min. Disabling a specified negative-feedback step leaves occupancy unchanged but cAMP is still 10 units at 8 min. The feedback step normally suppresses cAMP generation downstream of receptor activation. A separate supplied amplification model has one active receptor activating 20 enzymes, each generating 100 cAMP molecules in the measured interval.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the peak cAMP fold change, the percentage decrease from peak to 8 min with feedback and the cAMP output of the amplification model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why adaptation does not require loss of ligand binding and why the intervention supports feedback.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish amplification from positive feedback and propose one measurement needed to assess specificity.

steps.text: Peak cAMP is 10.0-fold baseline and falls 80.0% from peak.
The supplied amplification model generates 2000 cAMP molecules per active receptor in the interval.
Receptor occupancy stays high while cAMP declines, so dissociation of all ligand is not required for the response to weaken.
Disabling the stated downstream feedback preserves the high cAMP level, supporting a causal role for feedback suppression in this model.
Amplification means one upstream event produces many downstream molecules; it need not feed back to increase its own initiating activity.
Positive feedback specifically reinforces the upstream process, whereas this feedback suppresses cAMP generation.

title: Voltage-gated events explain a spike without using the pump as a reset switch
stem:
A schematic membrane-potential trace has values −70, −55, +30, −70, −80 and −70 mV at 0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 and 5.0 ms. Threshold is −55 mV. A selective voltage-gated Na+ channel blocker prevents the rapid rising phase without directly blocking the sodium–potassium pump. All values are relative to the outside.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the change from rest to peak and identify the phases from 0.5 to 1.0 ms and 1.0 to 2.0 ms.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the main ion movements responsible for those phases and the undershoot.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish the pump’s role and explain why immediately re-exciting the membrane is limited.

steps.text: Peak−rest = 30−(−70).
The change is +100 mV; 0.5–1.0 ms is rapid depolarization and 1.0–2.0 ms is repolarization.
Threshold activation opens voltage-gated Na+ channels, allowing Na+ influx down its electrochemical gradient.
Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels allow K+ efflux, repolarizing the membrane.
Some K+ channels remain open briefly, causing the membrane to become more negative than rest before it returns.
The sodium–potassium pump maintains ion gradients over time; it is not the direct rapid mechanism that produces each repolarizing phase.
Recently inactivated Na+ channels cannot immediately reopen, creating a refractory interval.
The blocker evidence supports Na+-channel involvement in the rising phase, but does not by itself quantify the pump’s long-term contribution.

title: Myelin changes where action potentials are regenerated
stem:
A myelinated axon has successive excitable nodes 2.00 mm apart. The action-potential peak reaches node 1 at 0, node 2 at 0.040 ms and node 3 at 0.080 ms. When the segment between nodes 2 and 3 is demyelinated, arrival at node 3 is delayed to 0.240 ms; node 2 remains at 0.040 ms. Treat these times as conduction delays after equipment correction.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate speed between nodes 2 and 3 before and after demyelination.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain saltatory conduction without claiming that a material particle jumps between nodes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict a possible severe effect of demyelination and identify two variables for a fair experiment.

steps.text: Normal speed = 50.0 m s−1; demyelinated speed = 10.0 m s−1.
Action potentials generate local currents that depolarize the next excitable region.
Myelin reduces current loss across internodal membrane, so threshold can be reached efficiently at the next node.
The action potential is regenerated at nodes; ions themselves do not travel the full inter-node distance as a single jumping packet.
Increased current leakage can leave the next node below threshold, causing conduction failure as well as slowing.
Keep axon diameter and temperature constant, and compare the same path length with matched recording positions.
Use independent axons and verify myelin damage rather than attributing all delay changes to myelin when nodal channels or cell viability may also be affected.

title: Excitatory and inhibitory inputs combine before threshold
stem:
A constructed postsynaptic integration model starts at −70 mV with threshold −55 mV. A single excitatory input E causes a brief +6 mV change; a simultaneous inhibitory input I causes −8 mV. Within the specified short window, the model sums voltage changes linearly. Outside that window each effect has decayed. This is a supplied approximation for small postsynaptic potentials, not a claim that action-potential amplitudes add.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Predict whether three simultaneous E inputs reach threshold, and whether the same three E inputs plus I reach it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Distinguish spatial from temporal summation using this model.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain inhibition and evaluate two limits of the linear calculation.

steps.text: Three E inputs reach threshold; three E plus I do not.
Spatial summation combines inputs from different presynaptic neurons arriving at the same time.
Temporal summation combines sufficiently closely spaced inputs from the same presynaptic source before earlier potentials decay.
An inhibitory input moves potential farther from threshold or reduces the effect of excitation, decreasing the probability of firing.
Real effects depend on synapse location, conductance and timing, so equal arithmetic changes are a model simplification.
Once threshold triggers an action potential, its amplitude is not the sum of EPSP amplitudes; firing probability/frequency changes rather than creating a 3× action potential.
Inputs separated by more than the decay window do not sum as assumed here.

title: Blocking dopamine reuptake changes how long a synaptic signal persists
stem:
In a constructed dopamine synapse, equal transmitter release occurs at t=0. Extracellular dopamine concentration is 100, 37, 14 and 5 units at 0, 1, 2 and 3 s in control conditions, and 100, 74, 55 and 41 with a cocaine treatment that selectively blocks reuptake in this model. Receptor response remains above a supplied activation threshold when dopamine exceeds 20 units. Release is not repeated during the interval.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the sampled values to identify the last sampled time above threshold in each condition and calculate the treated/control concentration ratio at 3 s.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the mechanism without assuming more transmitter was released.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the inference about signalling and its limits.

steps.text: Control is above threshold at 1 s but not 2 s; treated is still above threshold at 3 s.
The 3 s concentration ratio is 8.20.
Reuptake normally removes dopamine from the synaptic region into the presynaptic side.
