title: Stimulus intensity can be encoded by spike frequency, not spike height
stem:
A pain-receptor model is recorded over equal 0.200 s windows. A weak stimulus produces 4 action potentials and a strong stimulus 14. Peak amplitude is approximately 100 mV in both. A selective local Na+-channel block eliminates spikes, while a nearby unblocked receptor still responds. The experiment measures peripheral receptor output, not a direct report of subjective experience.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.prompt: Calculate the firing frequencies and their ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the distinction between action-potential amplitude and frequency encoding.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate what the block and recording establish about pain and consciousness.

steps.text: Frequency = count/window duration: 4/0.200 and 14/0.200.
Frequencies are 20.0 and 70.0 Hz; strong/weak ratio = 3.50.
An individual triggered action potential is approximately all-or-none, so a stronger stimulus need not make each spike taller.
A stronger effective stimulus can cause threshold to be reached more often, increasing spike frequency.
Refractory recovery limits how frequently the same axon can generate separate action potentials.
Loss of spikes after the selective block supports a role for local voltage-gated Na+ channels in transmitting the receptor output.
A working neighbouring receptor helps control for general failure of the recording conditions but does not test every off-target effect.
Peripheral spike frequency is input to central processing; subjective pain/conscious experience emerges from nervous-system activity and cannot be read off this one receptor trace alone.

title: Tip shading and an auxin barrier test different stages of phototropism
stem:
Identical shoots receive light from the left. Mean curvature toward light after 4 h is 30° for intact tips, 2° for opaque tip caps and 28° for transparent caps. In separate shoots, an impermeable barrier under the tip on the shaded side gives 3°, while the same barrier on the lit side gives 25°. Each treatment has 12 independent shoots; reported values are means, not confidence limits. The schematic shows direction only, not the measured angles.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare the two cap treatments and calculate the reduction caused by the shaded-side barrier relative to intact shoots.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain a mechanism consistent with stronger effects of the shaded-side barrier.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate controls and a limitation of the evidence.

steps.text: Opaque caps largely suppress curvature while transparent caps preserve a response close to intact shoots, supporting a need for light perception at the tip.
The shaded-side barrier reduces mean curvature by 90.0%.
Lateral light leads to unequal auxin distribution, with greater auxin effect on the shaded side of a shoot.
Coordinated placement of auxin efflux carriers supports directional movement and maintains tissue concentration gradients.
Greater shaded-side cell elongation bends the shoot toward the light; blocking movement on that side disrupts the asymmetry.
The transparent cap controls for mechanical covering while allowing light; the lit-side barrier helps distinguish barrier placement from a general barrier effect.
Directly measure auxin distribution or carrier localization and elongation on both sides, because curvature alone does not prove the full molecular route.
Means and sample size alone do not establish statistical significance; report variation and an appropriate analysis of independent shoots.

title: An acidic wall can bypass one auxin-dependent growth step
stem:
A constructed shoot-segment experiment supplies turgor-supporting conditions and measures elongation over 2 h. Control segments elongate 1.0 mm, auxin-treated segments 4.0 mm, auxin plus a selective inhibitor of plasma-membrane H+ secretion 1.2 mm, and inhibitor plus an externally acidified cell wall 3.6 mm. The inhibitor does not remove cell viability or turgor. Root-tip-produced cytokinin and shoot-tip-produced auxin are also shown as transported signals in a separate schematic context.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the fraction of the auxin-induced extra elongation restored by external acidification relative to the control.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain acid growth and the bypass result.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain hormone coordination and evaluate a limit of the causal conclusion.

steps.text: Auxin extra growth = 4.0−1.0=3.0 mm; acidified-wall extra = 3.6−1.0=2.6 mm.
Restored fraction = 2.6/3.0 = 0.867, or 86.7%.
Auxin promotes H+ secretion into the apoplast, lowering cell-wall pH.
Wall acidification promotes loosening of cross links between cellulose-containing wall components, allowing turgor-driven elongation.
External acidification can bypass the inhibited H+-secretion step, supporting wall pH as part of the auxin growth mechanism under these conditions.
Shoot tips produce auxin transported toward roots, while root tips produce cytokinin transported toward shoots, coordinating growth across organs.
The balance of these signals can influence root versus shoot growth; one local elongation assay does not by itself describe the entire plant response.
The rescue is partial and conditional on maintained turgor/viability; independent replication and direct wall-pH measurement are needed, and acidification alone need not reproduce every auxin effect.

title: An ethylene pulse can trigger a self-reinforcing ripening response
stem:
Matched unripe fruits receive a 1 h ethylene pulse, after which external ethylene is removed. Their own ethylene production at 0, 12, 24 and 36 h is 1, 3, 8 and 12 units. Controls without the pulse remain at 1, 1, 2 and 2. Fruits receiving the pulse plus a selective inhibitor of ethylene perception remain at 1, 1, 1 and 2. All chambers are ventilated identically after the pulse and production is normalized per kilogram fruit.

All data are constructed for this original practice question; diagrams are schematic, not micrographs. Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures unless stated otherwise.

parts.prompt: Calculate the 36 h production ratio for pulsed versus unpulsed fruit and describe the effect of receptor inhibition.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain positive feedback in this ripening model and distinguish it from residual external gas alone.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate one strength and two limits of the causal claim.

steps.text: The production ratio is 6.00; perception inhibition largely prevents the rising response despite the same initial pulse.
Ethylene perception stimulates processes that increase ripening and further endogenous ethylene production.
The new ethylene can reinforce the same response, amplifying the initiating signal through positive feedback.
External gas is removed and ventilation is matched, so continued production measured later is not simply the original pulse remaining in one closed chamber.
The perception-inhibitor comparison tests dependence on sensing the signal rather than only correlation between ethylene and ripening.
Check inhibitor specificity and fruit viability; an unhealthy fruit could fail to produce ethylene for reasons other than selective feedback blockade.

Use independent fruits matched for species, developmental stage and temperature, and measure ripening as well as gas production; the supplied gas time course alone does not establish every feature of ripening.
